{{DISPLAYTITLE:Checking instead of convincing}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments|Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel}}

Mathematics accepts a proof when the people competent to judge it are convinced.
This page describes how that works, two well-documented cases in which it came
under strain, what a mechanical check adds to it, and the principle, known as
'''de Bruijn's criterion''', that keeps a mechanical checker small enough to be
trusted itself.

== How a proof is accepted ==

A proof written for a journal does two jobs at once. It '''convinces''': it gives
enough steps for a reader to verify, one by one, that the statement holds. And it
'''explains''': it shows why the statement is true, and how one might have found
the argument.<ref name="geuvers2009">Herman Geuvers, "Proof assistants: history, ideas and future", ''Sādhanā'' 34 (1), 2009, pp. 3–25. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s12046-009-0001-5 doi:10.1007/s12046-009-0001-5]</ref>

Acceptance runs through people. A journal sends the paper to experts, the
'''referees''', who read it, test the steps they doubt, and report. If they are
satisfied, the paper is published, and other mathematicians read it, use it and
sometimes find faults later. The arrangement rests on a reasonable bet: one reader
may overlook a mistake, but many readers are unlikely to overlook the same
one.<ref name="geuvers2009" />

For most proofs this works well. It strains when a proof is too long or too
computational for a person to read in full, or when too few people have read it at
all.

== The Kepler conjecture ==

In 1611 Johannes Kepler stated that no way of packing equal balls in space is
denser than the familiar stack in which greengrocers pile oranges, the
face-centred cubic packing. Thomas Hales, working with Samuel Ferguson, settled
the question in 1998.<ref name="flyspeck">Thomas Hales and 21 co-authors, "A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture", ''Forum of Mathematics, Pi'' 5, e2, 2017. [https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2017.1 doi:10.1017/fmp.2017.1]; preprint [https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.02155 arXiv:1501.02155].</ref> The argument reduced the problem to
about a thousand complicated inequalities, which Hales checked with computer
programs.<ref name="geuvers2009" />

The referees were in a difficult position. Checking the inequalities by hand was
out of reach, and checking the programs themselves was never
attempted.<ref name="geuvers2009" /> After years of work they reported a strong
conviction that the approach was essentially correct, having found the specific
claims they examined to be right; but they could not certify every step. The proof
was published without that certification.<ref name="flyspeck" /><ref name="hales2005">Thomas C. Hales, "A proof of the Kepler conjecture", ''Annals of Mathematics'' 162 (3), 2005, pp. 1065–1185. [https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2005.162.1065 doi:10.4007/annals.2005.162.1065]</ref>

Hales answered by setting out to check the whole proof by machine. He announced
the '''Flyspeck''' project in 2003. It used two proof assistants, HOL Light and
Isabelle, and formalised both the written argument and the computer
calculations. The nonlinear inequalities were checked with HOL Light in July and
August 2014, and checked again that October on different machines, with identical
results.<ref name="flyspeck" />

== A proof only its authors had read ==

In December 2020 Peter Scholze asked for a theorem of his and Dustin Clausen's to
be checked in Lean. He counted it among his most important results, others
would rely on it without rereading it, and nobody besides its authors had gone
through the details; he wrote that he still had small doubts.<ref name="scholze2020">Peter Scholze, "Liquid tensor experiment", guest post on the ''Xena'' blog, 5 December 2020. [https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2020/12/05/liquid-tensor-experiment/ xenaproject.wordpress.com] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>

A group led by Johan Commelin completed the check of the main proof on 28 May
2021. The work found some imprecisions and oversights, each repaired with minor changes, and Scholze
wrote afterwards that he had no remaining doubts about the main
proof.<ref name="scholze2021">Peter Scholze, "Half a year of the Liquid Tensor Experiment: amazing developments", guest post on the ''Xena'' blog, 5 June 2021. [https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2021/06/05/half-a-year-of-the-liquid-tensor-experiment-amazing-developments/ xenaproject.wordpress.com] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> The history page on
[[Lean theorem prover/History/The Liquid Tensor Experiment|the Liquid Tensor Experiment]]
tells the story.

== What a mechanical check adds ==

'''Every step, not a sample.''' A referee reads with judgement and tests what looks
doubtful. A proof assistant checks every step, including the dull ones, and
cannot be tired or hurried.

'''The same verdict for every reader.''' Anyone can run the check again and get
the same answer. The verdict does not depend on who wrote the proof, how famous
they are, or how patient the reader is.

'''A smaller question for people.''' Once the steps are checked, specialist
judgement is needed for a much smaller part of the work. The Flyspeck authors put
it this way: a proof assistant largely takes the mathematical referees out of the
verification, but someone must still confirm that the statement proved is the
theorem everyone means, and that no unapproved axioms were
added.<ref name="flyspeck" /> The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]
is about that remaining question.

'''What it does not add.''' A mechanical check convinces; it does not explain. Its
level of detail is usually a hindrance to understanding why a theorem
holds.<ref name="geuvers2009" /> Nor does it end doubt for ever. A checker is a
program, and a machine-checked proof may still be faulty; the most that can be
done is to make that as unlikely as possible.<ref name="geuvers2009" />

== De Bruijn's criterion ==

That last point raises an obvious objection. If the checker is a large and
complicated program, there is no clear reason to trust it more than a careful
referee.

An answer goes back to '''Automath''', a project begun by Nicolaas de Bruijn in
1967.<ref name="geuvers2009" /> The idea is to separate the work in two. The large,
clever program that helps a person write a proof should also produce a complete
record of it, a '''proof object''' in which every step is explicit. A second
program, small and simple, then checks that record. It should be simple enough
that a sceptical reader could write such a checker for themselves. Henk Barendregt
named this requirement the '''de Bruijn criterion'''.<ref name="geuvers2009" />

The effect is that trust no longer depends on the size of the system. The parts
that search, guess and automate may be large and may contain faults; a fault there
can stop a proof from being found, but whatever they produce is checked by the
small program before it is accepted.

Lean is built this way. A finished Lean proof is a term that records the whole
argument, enough to be checked independently.<ref name="ref-types">The Lean Developers, "The type system", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/The-Type-System/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/The-Type-System/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> The part of
Lean that has the last word, Lean's kernel, was meant from the start to be small
and independently implementable, and independent implementations of it
exist.<ref name="ref-intro">The Lean Developers, "Introduction", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0, section 1.1, "History". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Introduction/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Introduction/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> The pages on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/The small trusted core|the small trusted core]] and
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking a proof again later|checking a proof again later]]
describe both.

What the small checker checks is a proof written in a particular logic. The next
page describes the idea at the centre of that logic: that a statement can be
treated as a type, and its proof as a thing of that type.
